chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: The Mozilla documentation defines a closure as a combination of a function together with

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: references to its surrounding state.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: The easy definition is, a closure gives you access to anything outside of the current

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: scope.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: In JavaScript, closures are created every time a function is created.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: So this function is a closure and of course it has access to the variables within it.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: But if we move the variable outside of the function, we can see that it still has access

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: to the variable.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: So here the function scope is a closure, but the global scope can also be accessed within

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: the function.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: Here is another example.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: Suppose we have a counter and we want the counter to be available to all functions.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: We could use a global variable along with a function to increase the counter.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: The problem here is that any code on the page could change the counter without calling the

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: add function.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: So the variable should be local to the add function to protect it.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: So we could move the variable within the function and then return the counter, but this will

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: not work because we reset the local counter every time we call the function.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: An inner function can solve this.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: When nesting functions in JavaScript, all functions have access to the scope above them

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: because of closures.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: Here the plus function has access to the counter variable in the parent function.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: We're almost there, but not quite yet.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: We can't access the plus function from outside, and we're still resetting the counter every

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: time we call the function.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: This is where self-invoked functions come in handy.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: We'll change this into the variable add and define it as a self-invoked function by adding

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: the parentheses at the end.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: Because of this, the function will only run once, resetting the counter to zero and returning

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: a function expression.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: Now when we call the add function, we are accessing the inner function, but still have

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: access to the counter in the parent scope, even after the parent function has closed.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: All because of closures.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: JavaScript does not have a native way of creating a private method or variable, but by using

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: closures we can emulate private variables.

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: Now the counter is protected by the scope of the anonymous function and can only be

chunks.title: JavaScript Closures
chunks.text: changed using the add function.

text: The Mozilla documentation defines a closure as a combination of a function together with references to its surrounding state. The easy definition is, a closure gives you access to anything outside of the current scope. In JavaScript, closures are created every time a function is created. So this function is a closure and of course it has access to the variables within it. But if we move the variable outside of the function, we can see that it still has access to the variable. So here the function scope is a closure, but the global scope can also be accessed within the function. Here is another example. Suppose we have a counter and we want the counter to be available to all functions. We could use a global variable along with a function to increase the counter. The problem here is that any code on the page could change the counter without calling the add function. So the variable should be local to the add function to protect it. So we could move the variable within the function and then return the counter, but this will not work because we reset the local counter every time we call the function. An inner function can solve this. When nesting functions in JavaScript, all functions have access to the scope above them because of closures. Here the plus function has access to the counter variable in the parent function. We're almost there, but not quite yet. We can't access the plus function from outside, and we're still resetting the counter every time we call the function. This is where self-invoked functions come in handy. We'll change this into the variable add and define it as a self-invoked function by adding the parentheses at the end. Because of this, the function will only run once, resetting the counter to zero and returning a function expression. Now when we call the add function, we are accessing the inner function, but still have access to the counter in the parent scope, even after the parent function has closed. All because of closures. JavaScript does not have a native way of creating a private method or variable, but by using closures we can emulate private variables. Now the counter is protected by the scope of the anonymous function and can only be changed using the add function. This has been a 90-ish second JavaScript January.
